patch.objective: Recognizing signs of cardiopulmonary distress that require stopping treatment and notifying the supervising PT
secondaryObjectives: Monitoring vital signs and activity tolerance during a treatment session and responding to abnormal findings

sources.note: Relayed from the DPT case icu-early-mobility, not re-read for this band; its note: Read 2026-11-11 through a text extraction of the PDF. Normal exercise response: HR rises about 10 beats/min per MET and returns to the pre-exercise level in 3-5 min; SBP rises about 10 mmHg per MET. Stop criteria include SBP drop >10 mmHg with increasing workload, new or worsening dysrhythmia, RR >40, unable to speak comfortably, SpO2 <90% or a drop of 4% or more (acute coronary syndrome), SpO2 <85% (lung disease); lung disease activity target 88-92%. Orthostatic hypotension: SBP drop >20 or DBP drop >10 mmHg within 3 min of standing. Beta blockers: lower HR with exercise and a dampened BP response; use the RPE scale in addition to HR.

sources.cite: Hodgson CL, Stiller K, Needham DM, et al. Expert consensus and recommendations on safety criteria for active mobilization of mechanically ventilated critically ill adults. Crit Care. 2014;18:658. doi:10.1186/s13054-014-0658-y
sources.note: Relayed from the DPT case icu-early-mobility, not re-read for this band; its note: Read 2026-11-11 in a copy of the published PDF (the publisher's own PDF link could not be fetched). FiO2 below 0.6 with SpO2 above 90% and RR below 30/min were considered safe for in- and out-of-bed mobilization; vasoactive drugs are not in themselves a contraindication but rising doses call for caution; the most conservatively scored parameter takes precedence; oxygen reserve should exceed the activity. The traffic-light figures were not readable in the text, so no HR or MAP limit is taken from it. Written for ventilated patients; applied here to a patient on high-flow oxygen.

brief.situation: 10:00 in the medical ICU. You are the physical therapist assistant, carrying out the physical therapist's plan of care. Mrs. Okafor, 64, is on day 3 of a stay for pneumonia with sepsis and is getting better. The plan of care and rounds set today's goal: out of bed to the chair.
handover: High-flow nasal cannula, 40 L/min, FiO2 0.45. Arterial line, peripheral IV.
Awake, calm, following commands. Lived alone and walked without an aid before admission.

Your supervising physical therapist evaluated her yesterday, wrote the stopping rules on screen into the plan, and is on the next unit by phone. Report to the PT after the session, and at once if you stop for a rule.
Her nurse is in the room and can help; the respiratory therapist is on the unit.
howItWorks: The clock runs in real time at the pace you choose: study pace (3x) or exam realism (1x). Pause any time.
Her heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation and breathing respond to each activity and recover with rest, as in a real session.
The stopping rules are on screen. A rule that is met now is marked and read out at once.
Early on you are asked to write your plan. Then a debrief scores what you did.
